articles.title: From “I want that” to “application sent”

body.support:
You’ve found a job or course you want. Here’s how to apply.

**1. List the documents.** Read the ad again. What do they want?
- a **resume**.
- a **cover email** (a short note about why you want it).
- maybe a form, or **referees** (people who can say you’re good).
- for TAFE: a **USI**, a free student number.

**2. Match the ad.** In your email, use their words. If they want “reliable”, show you are: “I haven’t missed a footy training all year.”

**3. Check it together.** Ask two people to read it. Fix the mistakes.

**4. Practise the interview.** Answer with an example: what you did, how you did it, and what happened.

**Keep these until you get the job:** your **tax file number** and your bank details. Don’t give them before.
body.core:
You’ve found an opportunity you actually want. Here’s how to turn it into an application, and an interview.

**1. List every document.** Go back to the ad and list exactly what they ask for:
- a **resume**.
- a **cover email** or letter: a short note about why you want this and why you fit.
- sometimes an application form, your availability, or **referees** (people who can vouch for you; always ask them first).
- checks or tickets the job needs, like a **Working with Children Check**.
- for TAFE and other training: a **USI** (Unique Student Identifier), which is free to create online.

**2. Match the ad.** **Tailor** your cover email to this one ad. Use their words, and give a real example for each must-have. If they want “reliable”, prove it: “I’ve worked every Saturday at the canteen for a year.”

**3. Check it together.** Swap with others. Does it answer the ad? Are the spelling, punctuation and contact details right? Fresh eyes find mistakes you can’t see.

**4. Practise the interview.** Most questions are really asking: “Can you do this? Will you fit in?” Answer with an example: **what** happened, **how** you handled it, and **what happened** in the end. Prepare one question to ask them too.

**Not yet:** your **tax file number**, bank details and super details are only needed **after** you get the job. Anyone asking for them before is a red flag.
body.extend:
Finding an opportunity is half the work. The other half is an application tailored to one reader, and an interview you’ve rehearsed.

**1. Identify every required document.** Re-read the ad or course page and list exactly what’s required: a **resume**; a **cover letter** or email; sometimes an application form, availability or **referees** (always ask permission first); any mandatory checks or tickets, such as a **Working with Children Check**; and, for nationally recognised training, a **USI** (Unique Student Identifier), free to create online.

**2. Tailor it.** Address the **selection criteria** directly, in the employer’s language, with evidence. “Reliable” becomes “I’ve opened the canteen every Saturday for a year without missing a shift.”

**3. Review it collaboratively.** Peer review catches what you can’t see in your own writing: missing criteria, unclear sentences, errors in spelling, punctuation or contact details.

**4. Rehearse the interview.** Most questions test two things: capability and fit. Answer with a specific example: the situation, what you did, and the result. Prepare a question of your own; it signals genuine interest.

**5. Know who you’re applying to.** Use reliable sources (their website, recent news) to learn what they do. Check the information is current.

**Sequence matters:** a **tax file number**, bank and super details belong in onboarding, **after** an offer. A request for them before an interview is a common sign of a scam.

caseStudies.title: The trial shift

body.support:
Sometimes, after you apply, a boss says: “Come in and do a trial shift.”

Is that OK? Do you get paid?

The **Fair Work Ombudsman** is the government group that checks bosses follow work laws. It says:

- An unpaid trial is only OK to **show a skill** the job needs.
- It should be **short**: only as long as it takes to show that skill.
- The boss must **watch** you the whole time.
.
If you’re doing **real work**, like serving customers, you should be **paid**.
body.core:
After an application, some employers ask for a “trial shift”. Lots of young people have done unpaid ones without knowing the rules.

The **Fair Work Ombudsman** is the government agency that checks workplace laws are followed. It has clear rules, including for cafés and restaurants:

- An employer can ask for an **unpaid trial** only so you can **show specific skills** the job needs.
- It must be **no longer than needed** to show those skills.
- You must be **directly supervised** the whole time.
.
If you’re doing **productive work**, like serving customers, making coffee for sale or cleaning up, it’s work. You should be **paid** for it.

Knowing this before you go in means you can ask the right question: “How long will the trial be, and is it paid?”
body.extend:
After an application, some employers, especially in hospitality, ask people to do a “trial shift”. Unpaid trials have been common, and many young workers don’t know where the legal line is.

The **Fair Work Ombudsman** checks that workplace laws are followed. It has published guidance for the hospitality industry. An unpaid trial may be legal only if all of these are true:

- it’s needed so you can **show specific skills** the job requires.
- it lasts **no longer than needed** to show those skills.
- you are **directly supervised** the whole time.

If you do **productive work**, like serving customers, making food for sale or cleaning, that’s a job, and it must be paid.

The practical skill is to ask about it politely before you agree: “How long is the trial, what will I be doing, and is it paid?” That’s not being difficult. It’s knowing your rights.

model.text:
**Subject:** Volunteer application: weekend dog walker

Dear Sam,

I’d like to apply to volunteer as a weekend dog walker at Second Chance Animal Rescue. I saw the role on your website.

You asked for someone who is calm with animals and reliable. I walk my neighbour’s two dogs every day before school, and I haven’t missed a day this year.

I can volunteer every Saturday and Sunday morning.

My resume is attached. My referee is my neighbour, Mrs Lee, and she’s happy for you to call her.

Thank you for reading my application.

Kind regards,
Taylor Nguyen
0400 000 000

teacher.overview: The boss course for Next Steps. Students identify every document a real application needs (resume, cover email, referees, checks, a USI for training, and what comes only after an offer), write a cover email tailored to the ad, review applications in a group, and do a mock interview with structured feedback. The case study is the Fair Work Ombudsman’s guidance on unpaid trial shifts.
prep: Print workbooks, with spare feedback tables.
Students need a real opportunity: from Job Hunt or Check the Course, or a volunteer or work-experience role. Have a few local options ready.
Make sure each student has a resume (My Resume) or time to draft one.
Optional: invite a local employer or careers adviser to sit on interview panels.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What they need
steps: **Hook (10 min):** two applications for the same job. Which gets the interview?
**Sort (10 min):** now or after the offer.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Write it
steps: **Model (10 min):** tailor an email to an ad aloud.

lessons.title: Lessons 3–4 — Check it, practise it
steps: **Group check (25 min):** read applications against the ad; fix.
**Mock interviews (45 min):** groups of 3 rotate; feedback tables.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** resume — with application; TFN — after the offer; cover email — with application; bank details — after the offer; referees — with application; super details — after the offer.

**Annotation:** 1 clear subject; 2 greeting by name; 3 which job and where seen; 4 matches “reliable” with proof; 5 availability (asked for in the ad); 6 what’s attached, sign-off and contact.

**Case study:** an unpaid trial must be only to show specific skills, no longer than needed, and directly supervised; productive work (serving customers, making food for sale, cleaning) must be paid; e.g. “How long is the trial, what will I be doing, and is it paid?”

realityCheck: **Applying for real is a big step.** Not every student is ready to send an application. The evidence is a complete, checked application; sending it is encouraged but their choice.
**Peer review needs structure.** Give each reviewer one job (check the ad’s must-haves, or check spelling and contact details) or feedback becomes “looks good”.
**Mock interviews can be stressful.** Let nervous students do the first one with you, or record answers privately (the solo option).
**Unpaid trials are common in hospitality.** Some students will have done one. Keep the discussion about rules, not about shaming employers or families.
**Works in a real class:** yes, especially with a guest interviewer. Students often send applications that week.
